item.title: The Red Centre Turns Art Into a Way of Experiencing Country
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Central Australia’s Red Centre has been named among Lonely Planet’s World’s Top 25 Experiences Hotlist for 2027, with its immersive art experiences earning the region a place on the global list. The recognition highlights a creative landscape that extends well beyond traditional galleries, from Aboriginal art centres and contemporary artists to outdoor painting and large-scale installations across the desert. In Alice Springs, Parrtjima transforms Mparntwe through light, art and storytelling, while Iltja Ntjarra (Many Hands) Art Centre offers visitors the opportunity to see Western Arrernte artists working in the tradition of Albert Namatjira.

Further into the Red Centre, art becomes inseparable from the landscape itself. Wintjiri Wiru uses drones, light and sound to share Anangu stories against the backdrop of Uluru, while Sunrise Journeys projects art and stories across the desert at dawn. Bruce Munro’s Field of Light at Uluru and Light Towers at Kings Canyon create another interpretation of the desert after dark, while Art Tours of Australia leads small-group watercolour sessions in the Tjoritja (West MacDonnell Ranges). Together, these experiences offer travelers different ways to encounter Central Australia’s creativity while gaining a deeper understanding of Country, culture and the region’s Traditional Custodians.

The Curated Take: What makes the Red Centre particularly compelling is that art is not confined to a designated cultural stop. It can emerge from an artist working in an art centre, a story carried through light and sound, or the act of sitting outdoors and painting the landscape itself. That makes art a pathway into understanding place, rather than simply another attraction to add to an itinerary.

item.title: Sydney Harbour Sets the Stage for a Summer on the Water and Vivid Sydney
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Sydney Harbour takes on an even bigger role in the city’s summer travel season as Captain Cook Cruises extends its sightseeing and Taronga Zoo experiences through March 2027. Options include harbour cruises between Circular Quay and Manly, hop-on, hop-off itineraries linking waterfront destinations such as Taronga Zoo, Shark Island and Manly Beach, and combined cruise-and-zoo experiences. The range gives visitors different ways to experience Sydney from the water, whether spending a full day moving between harbour landmarks or simply taking in the skyline from the deck.

Looking ahead to Vivid Sydney 2027, Captain Cook Cruises is also introducing dining experiences aboard Sydney 2000 during the festival, including multi-course à la carte and degustation menus. Selected evening cruises will combine dinner with views of Sydney’s illuminated waterfront, while participating vessels will themselves become part of the festival through official Vivid Sydney light installations. With the city transformed after dark, a harbour cruise offers a different perspective on the festival, shifting the experience from navigating the crowds along the foreshore to watching Sydney’s landmarks and illuminated precincts unfold from the water.

The Curated Take: Sydney Harbour is often treated as something travelers see rather than something they experience. These offerings make the water itself the itinerary, whether that means using the harbour as a way to explore the city during summer or turning it into a front-row seat for Vivid. For a destination already defined by its waterfront, that shift in perspective can make a familiar Sydney experience feel new.

item.title: Highway 101 Turns 100 With a New Central California Road Trip
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
As California’s Highway 101 approaches its 100th anniversary this November, Nomada Hotel Group is using the milestone to trace a contemporary road trip through the Central Coast. The route connects five historic and design-focused properties between the Santa Ynez Valley, San Luis Obispo and Paso Robles, linking wine country with coastal communities and historic roadside towns. Rather than treating the highway simply as a way to get from one destination to another, the journey highlights the distinctive character of the communities along the route.

The road trip also points toward the next chapter of Central California’s roadside culture. Nomada plans to add Pozo in summer 2027, transforming the historic Pozo Saloon, which has welcomed travelers since 1858, into a small encampo retreat with vintage Airstreams and spaces for vans and RVs. Set near a lake, hiking and horseback riding trails, the property will add a more deliberately rustic stop to the collection while preserving the saloon’s longstanding role as a gathering place for the community. Together, the existing hotels and forthcoming Pozo property suggest a version of the California road trip built around character, history and places worth slowing down for.

The Curated Take: The centennial provides a useful reminder that the best road trips are rarely about the road itself. Highway 101 has spent a century connecting California communities, and Nomada’s approach gives travelers reasons to experience those connections through historic properties, wine country and unexpected roadside places. It is a more experiential interpretation of the classic American road trip, where the stops become as important as the drive.

item.title: El Dorado Maroma Reaches a Decade of Independently Verified Sustainability
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
El Dorado Maroma in Mexico’s Riviera Maya has reached a significant sustainability milestone, earning EarthCheck Platinum certification after 10 consecutive years of certification. The latest audit was completed without observations, marking a decade of ongoing measurement, benchmarking and independent assessment of the resort’s environmental and sustainability practices. EarthCheck evaluates hospitality operations across areas including energy and water use, greenhouse gas emissions, waste and wastewater, ecosystem conservation, land use and social and cultural management.

The milestone reflects an approach that extends beyond individual environmental initiatives. Through Grupo Lomas’ Evolución Responsable framework, El Dorado Maroma’s sustainability efforts connect environmental stewardship with people, communities and responsible business practices. Programs across the wider organization include sea turtle conservation, native plant restoration, animal welfare and community initiatives, alongside the less visible work of managing resources, waste, purchasing and energy. Together, they illustrate how sustainability can become part of the operating structure of a resort rather than a collection of standalone guest-facing programs.

The Curated Take: The most interesting part of the Platinum designation is the decade behind it. Sustainability claims are increasingly common in luxury hospitality, but a 10-year certification history offers a different measure of commitment because progress is assessed over time rather than captured in a single initiative. For travelers who want luxury and environmental responsibility to coexist, that continuity provides useful context for understanding what happens behind the guest experience.

item.title: The Nam Hai Marks a Decade of Vietnamese-Inspired Luxury
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
This December, Four Seasons Resort The Nam Hai in Hoi An marks 10 years of evolving its interpretation of locally rooted luxury in Central Vietnam. Set across 86 acres along Ha My Beach, the resort has continued to refine its villas, dining, wellness and cultural experiences while maintaining a design language shaped by Vietnamese traditions. Recent villa renovations introduce lighter, contemporary interiors while retaining elements inspired by Hue garden houses, including timber roofs, feng shui layouts, elevated sleeping platforms and views toward the sea.

The resort’s evolution also extends to its culinary and cultural offerings. Lá Sen draws on the foodways of Central Vietnam, while NAYUU brings Japanese omakase to the region and beachfront Sol & Sao moves from morning coffee to Vietnamese tapas and evening cocktails. Beyond the resort, guests can explore Hoi An Ancient Town, the Imperial City of Hue and My Son Sanctuary, as well as fishing villages, artisan workshops and family kitchens. At the Heart of the Earth Spa, wellness is influenced by Vietnamese Zen traditions, with meditation, yoga and retreats complementing the resort’s broader emphasis on slowing down and connecting with place. The Nam Hai has maintained a Forbes Travel Guide Five-Star rating for eight consecutive years and holds two MICHELIN Keys in 2026.

The Curated Take: A decade is particularly meaningful for a resort whose identity depends on place. The Nam Hai’s evolution has not been about continually adding more, but about finding new ways to interpret Central Vietnam through design, food, wellness and experiences. That balance between refinement and regional character is what gives the resort staying power beyond the conventional luxury-resort model.

item.title: Perfection in Flaws
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Drip. Drop. Drum. Rain against the maroon cover. Rolling off to land on a wet shoulder. Under an umbrella never meant for two, we walk slowly to keep in time. The air is warm, heavy with moisture. We weave in and out of the small shops along Main Street, ducking under awnings before slipping into the National Baseball Hall of Fame—less for the stats, and more for a dry room and a chance for our wool coats to dry.

There’s no crying in baseball, and on paper, there’s no rain in Cooperstown.

When we set off in the morning, the mental itinerary played out in clear, cloudless high-definition: a sun-dappled picnic by the shore, ice cream dripping over a paper cup on a wooden bench, a slow, hand-in-hand stroll past 19th-century porches, and an afternoon drifting through a quiet museum or two. It was the quintessential upstate postcard—the version of a road trip planned like an AI mood board, storybook and pristine, before we ever turned the key in the ignition.

Instead, the sky gave us charcoal gray and a steady drizzle.

Yet when we emerged from the hall hours later, the downpour had softened into a gentle mist. We made our way down to the edge of Otsego Lake. The water stretched out still and glass-like, framed by low mist clinging to the tree line and a few geese prowling the damp shore for crumbs. Right then, the cloud cover fractured. A single shaft of pale afternoon sun broke through the gray, casting a warm, luminous glow across the far side of the lake—a light so sudden, heavy, and dramatic it looked almost staged.

Inside the quiet galleries of the Fenimore Art Museum, standing before the works of the Hudson River School, you begin to see 19th-century landscape painting for what it truly was: a sophisticated escape engine. As the Industrial Revolution swept across the American landscape, bringing clear-cut forests, iron foundries, and steam engines to the Hudson Valley, artists like Thomas Cole and Frederic Church didn't paint the smoke stacks. Instead, they retreated to their studios to engineer grand, composite canvases—stitching together sketches of different mountains, rivers, and skies to create an idealized, pristine wilderness that never existed in a single view. As the real world grew increasingly mechanized and dense, their art offered a stressed public an emotional sanctuary of untouched, luminous nature.

Two centuries later, our instinct in the face of rapid technological acceleration remains entirely unchanged. Where Church and Cole used oil pigments and composite sketching to fabricate an unblemished natural horizon, we now use artificial intelligence and prompt engineering to generate hyper-lit, flawless visual worlds at a keystroke. AI imagery is not a new digital anomaly; it is simply the modern iteration of the Hudson River School’s core impulse—a collective human longing to curate a pristine, frictionless refuge on a screen whenever our actual reality feels too fast, loud, or artificial.

Yet when we stepped back outside into the cool air, the mist over Otsego Lake offered a truth no curated canvas or generated pixel could match. Pulling up a photo on a phone screen—a rain-streaked selfie of us squeezed beneath that umbrella not built for two—the contrast was striking. Our hair was damp, our coats were slightly heavy with moisture, and the water behind us stretched out under a brooding, gray sky. But there, framed by the wet weather and the soft silver light on the lake, was a serene, undeniable smile lighting up our faces.

It was messy, unscripted, and entirely unprompted. The Hudson River School taught us to seek sanctuary in composite perfection, and modern technology promises us flawless, friction-free horizons. But standing on the damp shore of the Glimmerglass, wet shoes and all, the real lesson of travel becomes clear: a generated ideal gives us a dream, but true perfection is drawn in the flaws.

This piece is part of the latest issue of Curated Travel Magazine, where we explore travel through immersive stories, cultural insight, and thoughtfully curated experiences around the world.

item.title: Four Seasons Mumbai Takes a Contemporary Approach to Luxury
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Four Seasons Hotel Mumbai has earned a MICHELIN Key in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide hotel selection, distinguishing the property within a city known for some of India’s most elaborate historic and palace-style hotels. The Guide’s assessment highlights a deliberately contemporary interpretation of luxury, from the hotel’s glass tower and stone-clad lobby to interiors in subdued natural tones. Guest rooms keep the focus on the Arabian Sea and Mumbai skyline, pairing those views with marble bathrooms, soaking tubs and other modern comforts.

The hotel’s southern Worli location provides a convenient base for exploring or conducting business in Mumbai, while a two-floor spa and daily yoga offer a quieter counterpoint to the city’s intensity. Rooftop bar AER, all-day dining at Opus and personalized service add to the experience, with the upcoming SanQi restaurant set to bring another dimension to the hotel’s culinary offering. Together, the spaces reflect a version of Mumbai luxury rooted in contemporary design rather than historical grandeur.

The Curated Take: The MICHELIN Key is particularly interesting here because it reinforces that luxury in Mumbai does not have to mean recreating the city’s grand past. Four Seasons Hotel Mumbai offers a different proposition, one that uses modern architecture, expansive views and understated design to engage with the city as it is today. For travelers drawn to contemporary India, that distinction makes the hotel a useful counterpoint to Mumbai’s celebrated heritage properties.

item.title: Sevierville Reconstructs Dolly Parton’s Hometown Story
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
In Sevierville, Tennessee, visitors will soon be able to follow the early chapters of Dolly Parton’s story through the places that shaped her hometown years. In Dolly’s Footsteps, a new free self-guided walking tour, connects nine downtown locations associated with Parton’s childhood and early career, including the former theater where she performed her first paying gig and the site of Red’s Café, where visitors can hear Parton recall one of her early visits through video. The route begins near Sevierville’s Dolly statue and uses granite-and-bronze markers, photographs, videos and stories to bring the historic locations to life.

Developed by the Sevierville Chamber of Commerce with Sevier County Historian Carroll McMahan and in collaboration with Dollywood, the tour looks beyond the familiar Dolly Parton legend to explore the people and places of the community that surrounded her. Stops include former businesses such as Easy Way Five and Dime, Carr Dry Goods Co. and Raymond’s Shoe Store, along with Temple Milling Company, Kilpatrick’s Drug Store, the Old Post Office and The Pines Theater. While downtown Sevierville has changed since Parton’s early years, the tour aims to preserve the connections and memories that remain, offering visitors a more personal way to understand the town behind the global icon.

The Curated Take: Celebrity destinations can easily become exercises in collecting photo opportunities. In Dolly’s Footsteps offers something more meaningful by using Parton’s story as a doorway into Sevierville itself. Walking from storefront to theater to community landmark turns a famous life story into a sense-of-place experience, showing how an artist’s hometown can remain part of the story long after the person has left it.

item.title: Three Australian Retreats, Three Distinct Takes on Luxury
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Three hotels within Salter Brothers Hospitality’s Worlds Apart collection have earned recognition in the 2026 MICHELIN Key hotel selection, illustrating just how differently luxury can take shape across Australia. Newly relaunched Ardour Milton Park Bowral in the Southern Highlands received One MICHELIN Key, while Spicers Peak Lodge in Queensland’s Scenic Rim and Spicers Sangoma Retreat in the Blue Mountains retained Two Keys. The recognition comes as MICHELIN’s hotel guide continues to expand its presence across Australia, where properties are assessed for everything from design and service to character and connection to place.

The three retreats offer distinctly different experiences. Ardour Milton Park Bowral combines the architecture and gardens of a historic Southern Highlands estate with contemporary design, destination dining and wellness following its 2026 transformation. In Queensland, Spicers Peak Lodge pairs an intimate, all-inclusive experience with personalized service and the wilderness of the Great Dividing Range, while adults-only Spicers Sangoma Retreat offers secluded bushland, distinctive design and highly personalized stays in the foothills of the Blue Mountains. Together, they demonstrate the range of landscapes and experiences represented within the Worlds Apart collection.

The Curated Take: The interesting story isn’t that one collection has three MICHELIN Key hotels. It’s that the recognition doesn’t flatten them into the same idea of luxury. A historic estate, a wilderness lodge and a secluded bush retreat can all deliver exceptional hospitality while remaining deeply rooted in their individual settings. That distinction is increasingly important in Australian luxury travel, where the landscape and character of a property can be as integral to the experience as the service itself.

item.title: Regent Hong Kong Turns Victoria Harbour Into the Setting for Celebrations
item.dc:creator: Sandra Thomas-Comenole
item.content:encoded:
Regent Hong Kong has introduced The Terrace, a new semi-indoor, semi-outdoor waterfront venue overlooking Victoria Harbour and the Hong Kong Island skyline. Elevated above one of the city’s defining waterfronts, the approximately 290-square-metre space is designed so the harbour becomes part of the occasion itself, shifting from daylight over the water to a luminous cityscape after dark. The setting accommodates up to 250 guests for cocktail receptions and 108 for seated gatherings.

The Terrace is designed for weddings, private dinners, milestone celebrations, VIP receptions, product launches and brand experiences, with adaptable spaces that allow events to move naturally between covered and open-air areas. Bespoke layouts, floral design, menus and styling can be tailored to each occasion, while the venue’s location on Salisbury Road places it beside K11 MUSEA and within easy reach of Hong Kong’s commercial, cultural and entertainment districts. Together, the setting and flexibility give the new venue a distinctly Hong Kong quality, pairing the intimacy of a private celebration with one of the city’s most recognizable views.

The Curated Take: The Terrace works because the destination is doing much of the storytelling. Rather than treating the waterfront as scenery outside the event space, Regent Hong Kong has designed the experience around the changing character of Victoria Harbour. For travelers planning a significant celebration in Hong Kong, that creates something more memorable than a conventional ballroom: an occasion that evolves with the city beyond the windows.
